prompt: What is a serverless SQL pool billed for?

choices.text: Each hour it is available, at its size
choices.why: That is the dedicated pool; serverless has no size.

choices.text: The data its queries process
choices.why: Right: per terabyte, at least 10 MB a query.

choices.text: The rows each query returns to the client
choices.why: What is read, not what is returned, decides it.

choices.text: The files stored in the workspace's lake
choices.why: Storage is the storage account's bill, not the pool's.

prompt: Quitanda's dedicated pool runs one report a night, for an hour. What does a pool left running all day cost it?
hint: What does a paused pool bill?

choices.text: Twenty-three idle hours of compute, every day
choices.why: Right: paused, it would bill storage only.

choices.text: Nothing extra, since idle compute is not billed
choices.why: A running dedicated pool is billed by the hour, busy or not.

choices.text: Only the storage, as for a paused pool
choices.why: That is what pausing buys.

choices.text: The data it processes, as serverless does
choices.why: That is the other pool's meter.

prompt: What is the minimum, in megabytes, that a serverless pool bills for one query?
hint: Three of `ask.py`'s four questions fell under it.

prompt: Dashboards query three tables all day; analysts explore the rest of the lake now and then. Which arrangement fits?
hint: The two pools are not rivals.

choices.text: Load the whole lake into a dedicated pool
choices.why: Pays by the hour to hold what is rarely asked.

choices.text: Serverless for everything, dashboards included
choices.why: Possible, but every dashboard refresh is billed by its bytes, all day.

choices.text: A dedicated pool for the three tables, serverless for the rest
choices.why: Right: constant demand on provisioned capacity, occasional questions on the lake.

choices.text: Two dedicated pools, one paused at night
choices.why: The exploring still pays for a pool sized for it.

prompt: Into how many distributions is every table of a dedicated SQL pool split?
Quitanda hashes its orders table on `store`, which has five values. What happens to a query over it?

choices.text: It runs on all 60, a twelfth of the work on each
choices.why: Only distributions that hold rows have work.

choices.text: Five distributions do it all while 55 wait
choices.why: Right: skew, from a column with too few values.

choices.text: The pool rehashes it on a better column
choices.why: The definition is yours; nothing changes it.

choices.text: It is refused until a sixth store opens
choices.why: Skew is slow, not refused.

prompt: Match each table to the distribution that fits it.
hint: One kind of table fits none.

pairs.left: A large fact table of orders
A staging table loaded and read once
A small table of the five stores

prompt: Two large tables are both hashed on `customer_id` and joined on `order_id`. What does the query plan show?
hint: Are matching rows on the same node?

choices.text: Nothing special: both are hashed, so the join is local
choices.why: Hashed on a column other than the join's, matching rows can be anywhere.

choices.text: A data movement step
choices.why: Right: rows are shuffled so that matches meet.

choices.text: An error, because the join column must be the hash column
choices.why: It runs; it is just slower.

choices.text: A replication of both tables to every node
choices.why: Replication is a table definition, not something a query does.

prompt: Why were the same orders 40% smaller as Parquet than as CSV?
hint: How each format lays out a column.

choices.text: Parquet drops rows that repeat
choices.why: Every order is there; the counts matched.

choices.text: `gen.py` wrote fewer days of Parquet
choices.why: 31 files each.

choices.text: Columns compress; numbers stay numbers
choices.why: Right: CSV spells every value out on every line.

choices.text: Azurite compresses Parquet blobs on upload
choices.why: Blob storage stores bytes as given.

prompt: Folders named like `dt=2026-10-15`, which a reader turns into a column, are called ___ partitioning.
hint: Named after the system that made the convention.

prompt: What in a Parquet file lets a reader fetch two columns of seven?

choices.text: A header line naming the columns, as in CSV
choices.why: A header names columns; it says nothing about where their data is.

choices.text: The footer, saying where each column's data starts
choices.why: Right: read the footer, then seek to the blocks needed.

choices.text: The `dt=` folder it sits in
choices.why: The folder skips whole files, not columns.

choices.text: An index Azurite keeps beside the blob
choices.why: The storage knows nothing about the format.

prompt: To the nearest whole number, how many times fewer bytes did the Parquet month read than the CSV month?
The one-day Parquet query opened the file of 1 October as well as the 15th. Why?

choices.text: Partition pruning failed for the first day
choices.why: It worked: 29 days were never opened.

choices.text: DuckDB reads the oldest file to check the dates
choices.why: The dates are in the folder names.

choices.text: The 1st held orders of the 15th
choices.why: Each file holds its own day.

choices.text: To learn the table's columns
choices.why: Right: PyArrow reads one file for the schema when the dataset is made.

prompt: The one-day CSV query read about eight times the one-day Parquet query. What did partitioning do for the CSV?

choices.text: Two files opened of 31, as for Parquet
choices.why: Right: the folders decide how many files; the format decides how much of each.

choices.text: Nothing, because CSV cannot be partitioned
choices.why: Partitioning is folders, and works for any format.

choices.text: It let the reader skip columns in the CSV
choices.why: Folders skip files, never columns.

choices.text: It halved the bytes of the remaining file
choices.why: The whole of the 15th was read.

prompt: Three of the four queries would be billed the same 10 MB on a serverless pool. Why does the layout still matter?
hint: What grows and what does not?

choices.text: It does not: the minimum makes every query cost the same
choices.why: Only while the lake is tiny.

choices.text: Because the minimum is charged per file opened
choices.why: It is per query.

choices.text: The ratios grow with the data; the minimum stays put
choices.why: Right: a year read every five minutes is where 150 times matters.

choices.text: Because CSV queries are refused above 10 MB
choices.why: Nothing refuses them; they are billed.

prompt: Which of these did `ask.py` measure, and which belong to Synapse? Choose the ones `ask.py` measured.

choices.text: The bytes a reader had to fetch from the lake
choices.why: Right: counted in `readinto`.

choices.text: Which blobs a filter on `dt` let it skip
choices.why: Right: two opened of 31.

choices.text: The data processed that Synapse would bill
choices.why: That includes Synapse's own steps; the count is a lower bound.

choices.text: The time Synapse would take to answer
choices.why: Nothing here ran Synapse.

prompt: Why does the storage account in `main.tf` say `is_hns_enabled = true`?

choices.text: To make the pool's backups zone redundant
choices.why: Backups are `storage_account_type`, LRS or GRS.

choices.text: The workspace needs a Data Lake filesystem
choices.why: Right: the hierarchical namespace of lesson 3.

choices.text: So that serverless queries are free
choices.why: They are billed by bytes regardless.

choices.text: To let Azurite emulate it
choices.why: Azurite has no Data Lake endpoint, and Terraform does not talk to it.

prompt: Where in the declaration is the pool paused at night?

choices.text: In `sku_name`, by choosing `DW100c`
choices.why: That is the size while it runs.

choices.text: In `create_mode`
choices.why: That says how the pool is created.

choices.text: In the workspace's `identity` block
choices.why: That is who the workspace acts as.

choices.text: Nowhere: pausing is done outside the file
choices.why: Right: a schedule, a pipeline or a person.

prompt: `storage_account_type` accepts `LRS` and `GRS`. Why did Quitanda choose `LRS`?

choices.text: `GRS` copies backups abroad
choices.why: Right: to the United States, the paired region of lesson 1.

choices.text: `GRS` is not offered for pools at `DW100c`
choices.why: The provider offered both with no reference to size.

choices.text: `LRS` makes the pool pause faster
choices.why: Backups have nothing to do with pausing.

choices.text: `ZRS` was refused, and `LRS` was the next one
choices.why: The choice between the two offered is about where data may go.

prompt: Put in order what happened when `ask.py` answered the one-day Parquet question.
hint: The schema comes before the scan.
items: Read one file to learn the columns
Read the `payment` and `total_cents` blocks and add them up

prompt: A dashboard asks for today's sales every five minutes, over a year of orders kept as one CSV per month. What change saves the most?

choices.text: A bigger dedicated pool for the dashboard
choices.why: More compute, the same files read.

choices.text: Parquet, in one folder per day
choices.why: Right: one file opened instead of twelve, and two columns of it.

choices.text: Gzip the CSV files to halve their size
choices.why: Smaller files, still read whole, every one of them.

choices.text: Refresh every ten minutes instead
choices.why: Half the queries, each as wasteful as before.

prompt: Which statements about this lesson's practice are true? Choose all that apply.

choices.text: DuckDB answered every query, not Synapse
choices.why: Right: Synapse has no emulator.

choices.text: SQL Server refused a dedicated pool's `CREATE TABLE`
choices.why: Right: it does not know `DISTRIBUTION`.

choices.text: Terraform created a workspace with no account
choices.why: It validated a file and created nothing.

choices.text: The files were read through the Data Lake endpoint
choices.why: Azurite has none; they were read as blobs.
